subject: chemistry

moments.title: Lewis's cubical atom
moments.body: Lewis proposes the shared-electron pair as the basic chemical bond. In a paper drafted partly on the back of an envelope, he sketches atoms as cubes with electrons at the corners and bonds as shared edges. The octet rule emerges.
moments.takeaway: The shared electron pair, drawn on an envelope, becomes the central concept in chemistry.

moments.title: Lewis's textbook
moments.body: Lewis publishes 'Valence and the Structure of Atoms and Molecules', founding modern chemical bonding theory. He also formulates the broader Lewis acid-base concept the same year.
moments.takeaway: Lewis dot structures become the universal language of bonding.

moments.title: Pauling's resonance
moments.body: Pauling's 'The Nature of the Chemical Bond' uses quantum mechanics to ground Lewis's ideas. Hybridisation, resonance and electronegativity formalise organic and inorganic structure. Pauling wins the 1954 Nobel.
moments.takeaway: Quantum mechanics meets the curly arrow.

moments.title: VSEPR
moments.body: VSEPR (Valence Shell Electron Pair Repulsion) lets schoolchildren predict molecular geometry from Lewis structures: linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, etc. Simple, predictive, brilliant.
moments.takeaway: Molecular shape becomes a back-of-envelope calculation.

now.title: Where we are today
now.body: Lewis structures, VSEPR and electronegativity are universal teaching tools. Quantum chemistry calculations (DFT) now compute structures of millions of molecules. Both work.
now.open_questions: How accurate can semi-empirical bonding models be made? Can ML replace DFT?

reflection: Lewis was nominated for 35 Nobel Prizes and never won. He died (possibly by suicide) in his lab in 1946. Why does Nobel recognition sometimes elude the obvious?
